chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shammun from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Asam from Mis'ma ibn Abd al-Malik from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he (peace be upon him)
A man was brought who had stolen from the state treasury (bayt al-mal), so he (peace be upon him) said: 'He is not amputated, for he has a share in it.'
ai.seo_question: Why is the thief from the public treasury not amputated in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This ruling from Imam Ali (peace be upon him), recorded in al-Isfahani's *al-Istibsar*, establishes the principle of *khusūṣ al-ṣāḥib* (specific ownership) within the public treasury, distinguishing it from general public funds. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential view that the *bayt al-māl* comprises both communal resources and specific shares for individuals, thereby exempting the thief from the standard *ḥadd* of amputation if their personal share is taken. This nuance reflects the broader Shia emphasis on precise ownership rights in fiscal jurisprudence.
